To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

greater levels of currently felt negative emotion (i.e., anger and sadness) and subclinical mood symptomatology (i.e., anxiety and depression), respectively, predict greater DAN and DMN functional dominance.
Greater levels of currently experienced and subclinical negative emotions predict distinct patterns of functional coupling among the DAN, DMN, and FPC networks.

the intrinsic functional connectivity of the DAN, DMN, and FPC networks is modulated by the experience of negative emotions and subclinical mood disorders, and this may be related to variations in the cognitive and affective functioning of healthy individuals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the functional organization of the human brain supports the regulation of emotional experience and behavior.

the role of negative affect in shaping brain function and, more specifically, with the role of individual differences in the experience and regulation of sadness and anger in the functional architecture of the brain.
the neural correlates of inter-individual variations in the experience of affective states.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the DAN and FPC network are more active when the individual experiences negative emotions, whereas the DMN is less active.

the experience of sadness is associated with reduced DAN and DMN functional dominance and increased DMN-FPC functional coupling, whereas the experience of anger is associated with increased DAN and DMN (but not DMN-FPC) functional dominance.
the experience of negative emotions and subclinical symptoms are not only associated with functional connectivity in the DMN and DAN but also with functional connectivity in other networks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the functional architecture of the brain is shaped by the affective experiences of individuals, which in turn, are modulated by the functional architecture of their brains.
sadness, depression, and anxiety are associated with reduced goal-directed attention to the external perceptual field.

the experience of sadness is associated with a reduced capacity to attend to external perceptual information, whereas anger is associated with greater attention to external perceptual stimuli, and that this pattern may be reflective of the underlying dichotomy between the motivational orientations of withdrawal and approach.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in addition to their well-established roles in the pathophysiology of psychiatric conditions, the functional interactions between the DAN, DMN, and FPC networks also play a critical role in normal variations in the experience of affect.

the experience of specific negative emotion states and their associated subclinical mood symptoms may be associated with distinct functional neural signatures, which may be linked to variations in cognitive functioning, as well as to the development of affective and anxiety disorders.
the experience of negative emotions and subclinical mood disorders are not simply associated with aberrant neural activity, but rather with aberrant neural interactions.
